brief.situation: 20:00 on a surgical unit. Mrs. Okafor in Room 31, 68, 75 kg, returned from a laparoscopic right hemicolectomy at 15:00. The nursing assistant says she seems 'off' and her heart rate on the 20:00 check is higher than before.
handover: 17:00: heart rate 80, blood pressure 128/74, urine 60 mL an hour by catheter, pain 3/10 on hydromorphone PRN. Pulse oximetry on; vital signs every hour.
Hemoglobin 12.1 this morning; type and screen current. Enoxaparin 40 mg due at 22:00.
Standing orders: 500 mL lactated Ringer's bolus for hypotension, tachycardia over 100 or urine under 0.5 mL/kg/h, then call the surgical resident; stat hemoglobin and crossmatch by protocol.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Recognize what this is, act and escalate. Labs, blood and the operating room take time.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends by 22:00, then a debrief scores what you did.

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Names early postoperative hemorrhage from a rising heart rate, falling urine output, restlessness, cool hands and a fuller tender abdomen hours after surgery, with an anticoagulant due.
parts.modelAnswer: A heart rate climbing from 80, urine output falling from 60 mL an hour, new restlessness, cool hands and a fuller tender abdomen five hours after a hemicolectomy is bleeding until proved otherwise. She is compensating.

parts.label: Why act now
parts.criteria: Explains that the pressure falls late and the first hemoglobin lags; acts now: bolus by standing order, stat hemoglobin and crossmatch, SBAR that names bleeding and asks the surgeon to come and the enoxaparin to be held, blood when ready; no opioid in place of escalation.
parts.modelAnswer: Blood pressure holds until a large share of volume is gone and the hemoglobin lags, so waiting for either loses time. Start the bolus, draw a stat hemoglobin and crossmatch, and give the resident an SBAR that names bleeding and asks for a bedside review and the enoxaparin held. Hang blood as soon as it comes. An opioid for restlessness hides the warning.

arrest.headline: Arrest from an unrecognized bleed
arrest.body: The heart rate, urine output and restlessness changed long before the pressure. Find when each was noticed and when the surgeon was told.

orTarget.headline: Called before the pressure fell
orTarget.body: Urine output checked, a bolus, an SBAR that named bleeding, blood as soon as it came and back to the operating room while she was perfused. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: A rising heart rate, falling hourly urine output, new restlessness, cool hands and a fuller, tender abdomen five hours after surgery, with enoxaparin due, is early postoperative hemorrhage. The blood pressure falls late (class III) and the first hemoglobin lags, so act on the trend: start the standing-order bolus, draw a stat hemoglobin and crossmatch, and give the surgical resident an SBAR that names bleeding, asks for a bedside review and the anticoagulant held. Give blood as soon as it arrives (the restrictive threshold is for stable patients) and prepare her for the operating room. An opioid for restlessness without escalation hides the warning.

bpQ.ask: Her blood pressure is still normal. Why not wait for it to fall?

choices.label: A normal pressure means she has not lost much
The pressure falls late; heart rate, urine output and behavior change first

bpQ.explain: In the classic hemorrhage classes the heart rate climbs and urine output falls with a 15-30% loss while the systolic pressure holds; it falls in class III. Waiting for the pressure means waiting for a large loss.

choices.label: No: hemoglobin lags behind acute loss; act on the trend and repeat it

hgbQ.explain: Whole blood is lost at the same concentration, so the number barely moves at first and falls as fluid refills the vessels. A single normal value does not rule out early bleeding.
